judge_assessment.explanation: The judge's positive claims hold. I recomputed every value on the sheet from worksheet.tex and verify.json: 3.89+2.15 rounded to 4+2=6 (p1), 48.6+27.3 rounded to 50+30=80 km (p2), 50-(18.75+6.40)=24.85 (p3), 6*2.4=14.4 kg (p4), 0.85<0.89<0.9<0.905 (p5), 1.25-0.40=0.85 L and 1.25+0.40=1.65 L (p6), 6*5=30 (p7), 7.2/4=1.8 m (p8), 4.6*3=13.8 and 13.8>1.38 (p9), 3.75+2.8+4.05=10.6 km and 10.6-10=0.6 km (p10), 0.35*12=4.2 L and 4.2/0.6=7 (p11), estimate 4*7+3*2=34, exact 27.00+7.20=34.20, 34<34.2 and 40-34.20=5.80 (p12). The estimate entries also carry `place`, so the verifier really does round first, which is what the judge credited. Two things the judge did not look at, though, and both are visible in the delivered artifacts. (1) Problem 9(c) -- 'Which place value did Sam put his decimal point in by mistake?' -- is an explanation item; verify.json id 9 holds only the eval 13.8 and the compare '>', gate_log records no manual items, and final_response.md states 'Nothing on this sheet is left for a human to check.' The judge repeated that as an artifact finding ('Machine evidence reports no hard failures or manual items') rather than testing it against the printed page. (2) The judge scored answer_key_quality 4, but the key's Quick Answers bank prints '9. 13.8, --' and '12. 34, 34.2, --, 5.8': both dashes stand for relations that verify.json holds and passed ('>' and '<').

strengths_to_preserve: Problem 12 is a genuine synthesis: one problem carries four verify entries -- the rounded estimate 34, the exact total 34.2, the relation 34 < 34.2, and the change 5.8 -- and the key explains WHY the estimate landed low (the two markers were rounded down 40c each while the four paper packs were only rounded up 25c each). That is the estimate-versus-exact reasoning the task contract asked for, not a decorated sum.

Problems 1, 2 and 7 use verify type `estimate` with an explicit `place` ('whole', 'ten'), so the checker rounds each operand and then computes. An answer produced by computing exactly and rounding at the end fails the check, which makes the worksheet's own direction ('round first, then compute -- do not work out the exact answer and round it at the end') enforceable rather than aspirational.

The three declared traps are diagnostic rather than generic: 31.25 (subtracted only the first purchase, p3), 1.44 (decimal point one place too far left, p4) and 28.8 (multiplied instead of divided, p8) each print under 'Common wrong answers' with the misconception named, so a wrong number identifies a specific error.

root_causes.description: Coverage is enforced per problem id, not per printed answer slot, so an open-response sub-part on a problem that already has machine entries is invisible to the gate. Problem 9 prints three questions (a) exact product, (b) relation, (c) 'Which place value did Sam put his decimal point in by mistake?'; verify.json covers (a) and (b), id 9 therefore satisfies SKILL.md's 'every id 1..N has at least one check', and (c) ships as if verified.
evidence: worksheet.tex problem 9 prints '(c) Which place value did Sam put his decimal point in by mistake?'
verify.json has exactly two entries for id 9: eval a*b = 13.8 and compare [13.8, 1.38] -> '>'
answer_key.pdf p2 'Solution (c)' is a two-sentence prose explanation -- exactly the content SKILL.md line 257 reserves for type `manual`
gate_log.txt ends 'BUILD PASSED -- all gates green' with no manual-review line; final_response.md asserts 'Nothing on this sheet is left for a human to check.'

root_causes.description: render_quick_answers._fmt() hands every string `expected` to bare sympy.sympify(); sympify('>') raises and the except branch returns '---', the same glyph the module reserves for manual-only ids. Two verified relations are therefore deleted from the delivered bank.
evidence: verify.json id 9 compare expected '>' and id 12 compare expected '<' both passed (gate_log verify-ws PASS, 19/19 checks)
scripts/render_quick_answers.py lines 56-61: the str branch returns '---' on SympifyError; lines 71-73 return the same '---' for a manual-only id
The key body prints the relations correctly ('13.8 > 1.38', '34 < 34.2'), so only the at-a-glance bank is wrong

root_causes.description: \problem[<workspace>]{...} emits exactly one \ansline, so a multi-part problem that relies on the optional argument gets a single 3.5cm rule no matter how many answers it asks for. On this sheet problems 6, 10 and 11 hand-write one \answerline per part while 9 (three parts) and 12 (four parts) print one line between them.
evidence: templates/worksheet-preamble.tex line 89: \problem emits \ansline once, guarded only by \ifdim\mws@wsdim>0pt
worksheet.tex problem 12 is \problem[7cm]{...(a)...(b)...(c)...(d)...} -- worksheet.pdf p5 shows one 'Answer:' rule for four requested answers
worksheet.tex problems 6, 10 and 11 print two \answerline / \ansline macros each, so the sheet is internally inconsistent about the same layout question

improvements.title: Gate open-response sub-parts so an explanation on a machine-checked problem cannot ship unflagged
improvements.proposed_change: Add a manual-coverage gate to the build chain. A new checker (tests/check_manual_coverage.py, wired into scripts/build.sh beside answer-line-ws) segments the worksheet .tex with tests/_tex_segments.py and, for each problem, scans the printed prose for open-response cues -- 'Explain', 'Why did/does', 'Say why', 'What went wrong', 'describe', 'in one or two sentences', 'Which ... did/was' followed by a rule blank, and the drawing verbs 'Plot', 'Shade', 'Draw', 'label' -- and requires the matching id in verify.json to carry at least one entry of type 'manual'. Exit 1 with the offending sentence quoted when it does not. SKILL.md line 257 already states the rule ('Use manual for ... any explanation/reasoning answer'); nothing enforces it, and per-problem coverage (SKILL.md line 189) is satisfied by any single machine entry on the same id.
improvements.regression_test: tests/test_manual_coverage.py builds a fixture from this case: a worksheet segment ending '(c) Which place value did Sam put his decimal point in by mistake?' plus a verify.json whose id 9 holds only the eval and the compare. Assert the checker exits 1 and names problem 9. Add a manual entry for 9(c) and assert exit 0. Today the fixture passes the whole gate chain, so the test fails before the fix.
improvements.expected_impact: The delivered claim 'nothing is left for a human to check' becomes true or the item gets flagged. Graders stop treating a prose diagnosis as machine-proved, and the prompt's explicit instruction ('clearly label any genuinely open response for manual review') is enforced rather than trusted.
improvements.risk: A lexical cue list will fire on rhetorical prose inside an otherwise numeric problem ('Explain your check to a partner'), producing false manual flags. Keep the cue list narrow, require the cue to sit in a sentence that ends in a response slot, and let a top-level 'no_open_response' acknowledgement in verify.json suppress a reviewed false positive.

improvements.title: Print verified relations in the Quick Answers bank instead of an em-dash
improvements.proposed_change: Teach the Quick Answers bank to render a verified relation. In scripts/render_quick_answers.py, render_entry() should special-case an entry whose type is 'compare' with order 'relation': build the line from the entry's own `values` and `expected`, e.g. `$34 < 34.2$`, instead of handing the bare string '<' to _fmt(). _fmt() must stop returning '---' for a relation token, and '---' must remain reserved for items that carry no `expected` at all (genuine manual review), so the two states are visually distinct on the page.
improvements.regression_test: tests/test_render_quick_answers.py gains a case built from this case's id 12: entries [estimate 34, eval 34.2, compare values [34, 34.2] expected '<', eval 5.8]. Assert the rendered line contains '34 < 34.2' and does NOT contain '---'. Today render_entry returns '34, 34.2, ---, 5.8', so the assertion fails before the fix.
improvements.expected_impact: Both dashes on this key disappear and the bank again answers every problem. Across the suite, graders regain the ability to distinguish 'verified' from 'nobody checked this', which is the whole purpose of the reserved glyph.
improvements.risk: Low. The change is confined to one formatting function; the risk is a LaTeX escaping slip when a relation is typeset next to fractions, covered by compiling the fixture key in the same test.

improvements.title: Give every printed sub-part its own answer slot
improvements.proposed_change: Add a layout rule to tests/check_layout.py: within one \problem segment, count the printed sub-part labels ('(a)', '(b)', ...) and the answer-location macros (\ansline, \answerline, \ansblank, \noansline). Fail when a segment prints two or more sub-part labels and fewer answer slots than labels. SKILL.md's layout section should say that the \problem optional argument supplies ONE answer line, so a multi-part item must print its own line per part (as problems 6, 10 and 11 already do on this sheet).
improvements.regression_test: tests/test_preamble_layout.py gains a fixture reproducing problem 12 -- \problem[7cm]{...(a)...(b)...(c)...(d)...} with no explicit \answerline -- and asserts check_layout.py exits non-zero naming the problem; the same fixture with four \answerline macros must exit 0. check_layout.py has no such rule today, so the first assertion fails before the fix.
improvements.expected_impact: A student answering problem 12 gets four places to write four answers instead of one 3.5cm rule, and the sheet stops being internally inconsistent about the same question. This is the visual-quality dimension that scored 3 rather than 4 here.
improvements.risk: Sub-part labels also appear inside prose that does not ask for a separate answer ('(a) and (b) both use the same rule'), so the rule could false-fail. Limit it to labels that begin a sentence and let \noansline satisfy the count explicitly.

case_summary: A correct, well-interleaved decimal sheet: 19 checks over 12 problems, all recomputed here and all right, estimates verified as estimates rather than as rounded exact answers, three diagnostic traps printed as common wrong answers, and a two-page study guide whose four skills each carry a rule, a worked example and a distinct try-it (its own verify_study_guide.json has 10 entries, including the 0.6-versus-0.58 comparison). The ACCEPT is right. Three defects survive it, none caught by the judge. Problem 9(c) is an explanation with no verify entry and no manual flag, while final_response.md tells the parent that nothing needs human checking. The Quick Answers bank replaces two verified relations with the em-dash that the renderer reserves for unchecked items. And problems 9 and 12 print one answer rule for three and four requested answers respectively, while problems 6, 10 and 11 on the same sheet print one per part. final_response.md does name and describe all three PDFs, so the artifact-surfacing issue does not apply here.
